title: The mega backdoor and the pro-rata rule
teaches: How high earners put money into Roth accounts above the income limits: the backdoor Roth IRA, the pro-rata rule that can spoil it, and after-tax 401(k) contributions converted to Roth

blocks.text: Lesson 8 compared the four buckets by the tax rate going in and the rate coming out. For someone earning well at a large company, the comparison often favours Roth money. That holds especially for someone planning to stop work early, for two reasons. Roth money can be reached without the conversion ladder of lesson 9. And spending it adds nothing to income in the years when low income is worth most, for health credits and for converting other money in low brackets.

The direct routes are limited. A Roth IRA can't be funded directly once a couple's modified adjusted gross income passes $252,000 in 2026, or $168,000 for a single person; the amount allowed shrinks over the $10,000 or $15,000 below those lines.[^phase] The Roth side of a 401(k) has no income limit, but shares the $24,500 employee limit with pre-tax deferrals. Two indirect routes add more: the backdoor Roth IRA and, where the plan allows it, the mega backdoor.

blocks.caption: The most one person under 50 can put into Roth accounts in 2026 by each route, with an employer contributing $12,000 to their 401(k). The mega backdoor's room depends on the employer's contribution and on the plan.

blocks.text: Anyone with earnings can contribute to a traditional IRA ($7,500 in 2026), whatever their income. But for someone covered by a workplace plan, the deduction for it disappears at incomes far below the Roth limits, so a high earner's contribution goes in as after-tax money. Converting a traditional IRA to Roth has no income limit at all.[^rera] So the backdoor is two steps: contribute $7,500 to a traditional IRA without deducting it, then convert it to Roth. Since the money was already taxed, the conversion is taxed only on any growth in between, usually a few dollars. Those few dollars count as income for ACA credits too, which rarely matters, but a conversion of pre-tax money would.

Both steps are reported on Form 8606, filed with the tax return, which keeps a running total of the after-tax money in your IRAs, their **basis**, so it is never taxed twice. The conference report on the 2017 tax law, Congress's own explanation of it, described the two steps as allowed, so tax advisers no longer treat the backdoor as a risky reading of the rules.

The backdoor fails quietly for anyone with other pre-tax IRA money. A conversion can't choose to take only the after-tax dollars. The IRS treats all of a person's traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs as one pot, and every dollar converted is taxed in the proportion the pot is pre-tax, measured on 31 December of the year of the conversion.

Someone with a $92,500 rollover IRA from an old job, all of it pre-tax money from that job's 401(k), who adds $7,500 of after-tax money has a $100,000 pot that is 7.5 percent after-tax. Converting $7,500 makes $6,938 of it taxable. The backdoor has become an ordinary taxable conversion. The after-tax $7,500 isn't lost: Form 8606 carries most of it forward as basis in the remaining IRA, to be counted against later withdrawals or conversions, but it no longer does the job it was put there for.

The fix is to empty the pre-tax IRA by 31 December of the year of the conversion, by moving it into the current employer's 401(k), if the plan accepts money rolled in from IRAs. Even a December rollover rescues a conversion made earlier that year. 401(k) balances don't count in the pot. A spouse's IRAs don't count either: each person has their own.[^spouse]

A 401(k) has a second, larger limit: $72,000 in 2026 for everything going into one person's account, employee and employer together, not counting catch-ups, the extra contributions allowed from age 50. Some plans let employees fill the gap between their own deferrals plus the employer's money and that $72,000 with after-tax contributions. Someone deferring $24,500 whose employer adds $12,000 has $35,500 of after-tax room.

After-tax money in a 401(k) is a poor investment left alone: its growth is taxed as ordinary income when withdrawn. The mega backdoor works only when the plan also lets it be moved to Roth soon after it goes in, either by converting it inside the plan or by withdrawing it to a Roth IRA while still employed. Some plans do this automatically every day. Then only the small growth before conversion is taxed.

Whether a plan offers both features is in its summary plan description. Many large technology employers do; most small companies don't, because after-tax contributions make the plan's non-discrimination tests harder to pass.[^acp]

From 2026, anyone 50 or older whose Social Security wages from the employer were above $150,000 in the previous year must make their 401(k) catch-up contributions as Roth money: $8,000 a year, or $11,250 from 60 to 63. For most high earners near the end of a career this puts a little more into Roth whether they want it or not. The early-retirement plans of the main course would usually have chosen Roth for that money anyway.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Above the Roth IRA income limits, contribute to a traditional IRA without deducting it and convert: the backdoor.
Any pre-tax money in traditional, SEP or SIMPLE IRAs on 31 December makes most of the conversion taxable; roll it into a 401(k) first.
The mega backdoor fills the room left under the $72,000 limit with after-tax 401(k) money and converts it to Roth at once, if the plan allows both.
From 2026, catch-ups for those 50 or older whose wages from the employer were over $150,000 go in as Roth.

blocks.caption: Four questions on backdoor Roth contributions
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A couple earn $400,000. How can they get money into Roth IRAs?
choices: Contribute to traditional IRAs without deducting, then convert
They can't: they are over the limit
Contribute directly; the limit applies only to singles
items.why: Conversions have no income limit, so after-tax traditional contributions can be converted.

items.ask: Someone has a $92,500 rollover IRA and makes a $7,500 backdoor contribution. Why is most of the conversion taxable?
choices: The pro-rata rule counts all their IRAs as one pot
The rollover IRA is over the limit
items.why: 92.5 percent of the pot is pre-tax, so 92.5 percent of any conversion is taxed.

choices: Rolling the pre-tax IRA into a 401(k) before 31 December
Opening a second IRA for the backdoor
items.why: 401(k) balances don't count in the pot, and all IRAs count together however many there are.

items.ask: What two plan features does the mega backdoor need?
choices: After-tax contributions and a way to move them to Roth while employed
A Roth 401(k) and an employer match
items.why: Without the conversion, after-tax money's growth is taxed as income later.

summary: **High earners can't fund a Roth IRA directly.** Above an income limit set each year, the direct contribution route closes.
**The backdoor Roth goes through a traditional IRA.** Contribute without a deduction, then convert the money to Roth.
**Pre-tax IRA money spoils the backdoor.** Under the pro-rata rule it makes most of the conversion taxable, so move it into a 401(k) first.
**The mega backdoor converts after-tax 401(k) money.** Where the plan allows, after-tax contributions fill the rest of the total limit and are converted to Roth at once.

phase.title: The phase-out
phase.text: Direct Roth IRA contributions shrink between $242,000 and $252,000 of MAGI for a couple in 2026, and between $153,000 and $168,000 for a single person. Within that range a partial contribution is allowed.

spouse.title: One pot each
spouse.text: The pro-rata rule aggregates IRAs by person, not by household. Inherited IRAs and Roth IRAs are excluded. The balance that matters is the one on 31 December of the year of the conversion, so a rollover into a 401(k) in December still rescues a conversion made in March.

rera.title: How the backdoor opened
rera.text: Until 2010, Roth conversions were closed to anyone with modified adjusted gross income above $100,000. A 2006 tax act removed that cap starting in 2010 to pull conversion tax revenue into the ten-year budget window, accidentally opening the backdoor for high earners.

acp.title: Non-discrimination tests
acp.text: To keep its tax-favoured status, a 401(k) must show that highly paid employees don't use the plan much more than everyone else. A generous employer match lets a plan skip the test on regular deferrals, but voluntary after-tax contributions are tested separately under the Actual Contribution Percentage test, which has no simple opt-out.
